title: Claude, make my chart accessible.
text: Someone assumes data visualization means picking bright colors. It isn't that. Color has to encode something real, and the chart type comes first, chosen from what the data is actually doing. This runs on a skill a folder Claude

title: A skill is a folder
text: Reads before it acts. Inside one file lays out how raw data becomes a chart. Pick the chart type for the relationship in the data, write the plotting code, then apply the design and accessibility rules on top. The file is the whole program. The guide runs both ways. A ranking gets

title: The guide runs both ways
text: A horizontal bar. A composition over time gets a stacked area. Many variables at once get a heat map. And some charts are ruled out outright. Pie charts because people are bad at comparing angles, 3D charts because they distort the data, dual axes because they can imply a correlation that was never there. So color has to earn its place.

title: Color has to earn its place
text: One accent color carries the finding, everything else fades to gray. Red and green alone are out. About 8% of men can't tell them apart, and every chart has to survive in black and white. title: Your turn
text: A five-question customer survey, 1 to 10. Tell me what chart type this calls for and pick colors that would still make sense to someone who's color blind. Lay 'em in for bear. Data visualization isn't about making it colorful. Lay 'em in for bear.
